title: Randomized parity sketches versus one-way communication for XOR functions
formal: Are there universal constants \(C>0\) and \(a\geq0\) such that, for every \(n\geq1\) and every Boolean function \(f:\mathbb F_2^n\to\{0,1\}\), \[R^{\mathrm{lin}}_{1/3}(f)\leq C\bigl(1+R^{\rightarrow}_{1/3}(f^+)\bigr)\log^a(n+2),\qquad f^+(x,y)=f(x+y)?\] Here the two complexities use worst-input error and shared randomness as defined below. This fixes the polylogarithmic-loss convention in the source’s conjecture.
why: A positive result would justify proving lower bounds for arbitrary one-way XOR protocols by analyzing linear summaries, a much more structured class. A separation would identify Boolean information that a short nonlinear message preserves more effectively than nonadaptive random parities.
status_note: The primary CCC 2018 paper leaves the worst-input randomized comparison open. The checked April 2026 simulation is for a different streaming model and does not claim this one-way communication theorem. No matching resolution was located in the bounded 13 September 2026 check; the precise polylogarithmic-loss convention is stated explicitly.

progress.text: Yaroslavtsev presents the conjecture at the Banff workshop.
The CCC paper proves the uniform-distribution comparison and records the general randomized conjecture.
Jiang, Liu and Yu give a polynomial-length integer-turnstile simulation and distinguish prior XOR-stream results from that model.

importance.reason: A broad structural comparison between randomized communication and parity measurements, with consequences for transferring sketching lower bounds to unrestricted one-way protocols.

sentences: The input is an arbitrary Boolean function on a binary vector space.
A parity sketch measures a fixed random collection of linear forms and then decodes their bits.
A one-way protocol may instead send any randomized message about Alice’s vector to Bob.
The conjecture asks whether parity sketches lose only a universal polylogarithmic factor for the associated XOR function.
Known deterministic and uniform-input comparisons do not establish the required worst-input randomized bound.

definitions: The field \(\mathbb F_2\) has elements zero and one, with addition modulo two; vector addition is bitwise XOR. A randomized parity sketch of length \(k\) consists of a jointly sampled matrix \(A\in\mathbb F_2^{k\times n}\) and a decoder \(g\). Their joint distribution is fixed in advance, independently of the input \(z\). The sketch is the \(k\)-bit vector \(Az\); the decoder knows the sampled matrix and all shared coins, and may depend on \(f\) and \(n\). For each fixed \(z\), its probability of outputting \(f(z)\) must be at least \(2/3\). The minimum possible \(k\), including zero, is \(R^{\mathrm{lin}}_{1/3}(f)\). Each row of \(A\) specifies a subset of input coordinates whose parity is measured. Rows are chosen before seeing any measurement outcome: adaptive parity queries are not allowed. In the communication model Alice knows \(x\in\mathbb F_2^n\), Bob knows \(y\in\mathbb F_2^n\), and both know \(f,n\) and a public random string independent of their inputs. Alice sends one message; Bob must output \(f(x+y)\). For every fixed pair \((x,y)\), success probability is at least \(2/3\). The cost is the largest message length over inputs and coin outcomes; variable-length messages can be padded. Its minimum is \(R^{\rightarrow}_{1/3}(f^+)\). Local computation, the description of \(f\), and shared randomness are free in both models. No uniform polynomial-time construction of optimal protocols is required. Logarithms are base two. The constants in the proposed inequality are independent of the truth table of \(f\), the dimension and its communication complexity. The additive one handles zero-cost constant functions without imposing a convention for logarithms of zero.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the displayed inequality with fixed universal constants, or prove its negation: for every proposed constants there is a dimension and Boolean function violating the bound. A superpolylogarithmic separation family suffices for a negative answer. Equality for deterministic protocols, average error under the uniform input distribution, or a polynomial rather than polylogarithmic loss does not settle this target.

context_blocks.text: The source asks whether randomized linear sketching and randomized one-way communication of the associated XOR function agree up to polylogarithmic factors. The card spells out the usual dimension-based interpretation at error one third; it does not request exact equality of the two integer complexities.

The easy comparison is \(R^{\rightarrow}_{1/3}(f^+)\leq R^{\mathrm{lin}}_{1/3}(f)\): Alice sends \(Ax\), and Bob forms \(Ax+Ay=A(x+y)\) before using the decoder. The question is whether an arbitrary message can always be replaced, with the stated loss, by information of this linear form.

For deterministic exact computation the complexities agree. The randomized case allows a different error set for each choice of coins, so the deterministic statement does not give the desired simulation by simply fixing a seed.

Kannan, Mossel, Sanyal and Yaroslavtsev prove an analogue under uniformly distributed inputs, with an adjustment of the error constant, and analyze several function classes. Worst-input correctness is stronger: a protocol cannot ignore even a very small exceptional set of pairs.

The 2026 turnstile simulation paper concerns streams of integer-coordinate insertions and deletions. Its discussion treats modular and XOR updates as a separate line of work. A simulation for algorithms that already process long streams does not itself convert a single arbitrary Alice-to-Bob message into a parity sketch.
